卡爾尼克斯號具有明亮、尖銳且具有穿透力的音色，音質帶有某種金屬般的光澤感。其音域: The carnyx has a bright, sharp, penetrating timbre, with something of a metallic sheen. Its range is mainly the upper-middle register, and it can produce a loud, intimidating sound. Because it is made of bronze the instrument itself resonates well, and the sound spreads through the wide bell to project powerfully, which suits it especially to carrying outdoors on a battlefield. Compared with the modern trombone or trumpet, the carnyx sounds rougher and more primitive, with an excited, martial character and no warmth. Its distinctive S-shape projects the sound waves outward horizontally, which increases penetration and long-distance carry, and made it an effective tool for raising morale and for psychological warfare in ancient battle.
The carnyx is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 423.121.12, from Iron Age Celtic Europe. In antiquity it was used in war and ritual, and Polybius describes the din of horns at the Battle of Telamon. In modern reconstructions John Kenny has played it in concert halls, on radio, television and film, and in 2003 he played a solo at the Stade de France; in 2017 Christopher Gibbs commissioned a four-part song cycle, 《The Music of the Forest》, premiered at Sledmere village hall by the Blackburn Cathedral Renaissance Choir under the conductor Samuel Hudson, with Kenny playing the carnyx.

卡爾尼克斯號是鐵器時代凱爾特文化常見的氣鳴樂器，約西元前200年至西元200年間: The carnyx is an aerophone common in Iron Age Celtic culture, in use from about 200 BC to AD 200 and made of bronze in an elongated curved form. Its name comes from a Gaulish root meaning antler or horn. The Celts used it in war, and Polybius described its sound intimidating the enemy on the battlefield; it stands about 1.8 m tall and can be heard over a crowd. The Dacians used it as well as the Celts, and it also appears in Indian Buddhist carvings, which points to long-distance contact in the Iron Age. Its shape may have been influenced by the Etruscan curved horn; finds come from Scotland, France, Germany, Romania, Switzerland and Tintignac, and the Deskford find is regarded as a local Scottish variant, showing that ritual and military uses went together.

The carnyx is a bronze horn used in Iron Age Celtic culture, an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs classification 423.121.12. Its tube forms an elongated S: the central straight section is held vertically, and the mouthpiece end and the wider bell project horizontally in opposite directions, the bell usually shaped as an open-mouthed boar or another animal head. The player sounds it at the mouthpiece; the instrument is about 1.8 m tall and can carry over a battlefield or a ritual crowd. The Celts used it mainly in war, to urge their troops on and to intimidate the enemy; the Dacians used it too, and it appears in ritual settings.
